hops.afterHeading: The tug of war: where the voltage goes
hops.title: Why Sichuan peppercorns make your lips buzz
hops.text: Chili peppers burn. Sichuan peppercorns also make your lips buzz, though nothing is vibrating them. The cause is hydroxy-alpha-sanshool, which blocks potassium channels that are open at rest. With potassium's rope pulling more weakly, the voltage drifts up toward threshold. In isolated mouse skin, sanshool makes nearly every D-hair fibre, one kind of very sensitive touch receptor, fire with nothing touching the skin. In 2013, researchers dabbed ground pepper mixed in alcohol onto volunteers' lower lips, then had them compare the tingle with a vibration on a fingertip, over and over. On average the tingle matched a 50-hertz vibration: touch fibres reporting a buzz that was never there.

sources.citation: Bautista, D. M., Sigal, Y. M., Milstein, A. D., Garrison, J. L., Zorn, J. A., Tsuruda, P. R., Nicoll, R. A., & Julius, D., Pungent agents from Szechuan peppers excite sensory neurons by inhibiting two-pore potassium channels, Nature Neuroscience 11:772-779, 2008

Lennertz RC, Tsunozaki M, Bautista DM, Stucky CL, Physiological basis of tingling paresthesia evoked by hydroxy-alpha-sanshool, Journal of Neuroscience 30:4353-4361, 2010

hops.afterHeading: How three gates make one spike
hops.title: The poisonous bird that jams sodium channels open
hops.text: In the late 1980s, graduate student Jack Dumbacher was studying birds of paradise in Papua New Guinea when a hooded pitohui, an orange-and-black songbird caught in his net, scratched his hand. He licked the scratch, and his mouth burned and went numb. The next year he licked one of its feathers on purpose. Same result. The bird's skin and feathers carry homobatrachotoxin, one of a family of toxins also found in some poison-dart frogs and in small beetles that may be the birds' source. Batrachotoxins make sodium channels open at lower voltages and disrupt inactivation, so sodium current lingers and the membrane cannot reset for the next spike.

hops.title: Why a stubbed toe often hurts twice
hops.text: Next time you stub your toe, and you will, notice whether it hurts twice. Often a sharp jab comes first, one you can point to exactly. Then a duller, spreading ache arrives and stays. That classic sharp first pain is carried by thin, lightly myelinated fibres at roughly 5 to 30 metres per second. The ache rides bare C fibres at around 1 metre per second. Over the metre or so of nerve from toe to spinal cord, those speeds put the ache's signal about a second behind the jab's. Same toe, same kind of spike, two kinds of axon.
